text: Wassily Wassilyevich Kandinsky (16 December [O.S. 4 December] 1866 – 13 December 1944) was a Russian painter and art theorist active in Germany during the late Belle Époque and Interwar eras, widely recognized as one of the pioneers of abstraction in Western art. Born in Moscow to Lidia Ticheeva and Vassily Silvestrovich Kandinsky, a tea merchant, and with one of his great-grandmothers being Princess Gantimurova, he studied law and economics in school before beginning painting studies at age 30. In 1896, he moved to Munich, initially studying at Anton Ažbe's private school and later at the Academy of Fine Arts, where his teachers included Franz von Stuck; he had not been immediately admitted and began learning art independently. Before leaving Moscow, he saw an exhibit of Monet’s paintings, particularly Haystacks, which deeply affected him—though he could not recognize the subject, the painting’s vivid colour and emotional impact left a lasting impression. He was also influenced by Richard Wagner’s Lohengrin and Madame Blavatsky’s theosophy, which posited creation as a geometric progression through points, circles, triangles, and squares; these ideas are reflected in his writings, especially in Concerning the Spiritual in Art (1910) and Point and Line to Plane (1926). In 1902, he invited Gabriele Münter to join his summer classes in the Alps, and their relationship evolved from professional to personal. Kandinsky began to develop his theory of art as a spiritual experience, calling it "inner necessity," and later described a pivotal moment when he saw his own painting hanging upside down, which led him to recognize the power of abstraction. His early works, such as The Blue Rider (1903), The Blue Mountain (1908–1909), and Sunday, Old Russia (1904), show a move toward abstraction, using broad, expressive colour and flat planes, influenced by Fauvism and pointillism. In 1909, he witnessed Aleksandra Unkovskaya’s presentation on sound-to-colour synesthesia (chromesthesia), which inspired his concept of a chain reaction in art: "Emotion — sensation — the work of art — sensation — emotion," based on musical resonance. He began using musical terms for his works, calling spontaneous pieces "improvisations" and structured ones "compositions." He helped found the Neue Künstlervereinigung München (1909), which dissolved in 1911, and then co-founded The Blue Rider (Der Blaue Reiter) with August Macke, Franz Marc, Albert Bloch, and Gabriele Münter, releasing an almanac and holding exhibitions until World War I interrupted plans in 1914. His writings, especially On the Spiritual in Art, were influential internationally, with reviews in Art News (1912) and The New Age (1914), and his works entered British collections through Michael Sadleir, who acquired Fragment for Composition VII in 1913. From 1918 to 1921, he participated in cultural politics in Russia, helping establish the Institute of Artistic Culture in Moscow and promoting art education, though his spiritual and expressionistic views were rejected by radical members. In 1921, he was invited to the Bauhaus in Weimar by Walter Gropius, where he taught design, advanced theory, and painting from 1922 until the Nazis closed the school in 1933. He also signed the "Founding Proclamation of the Union of Progressive International Artists" in 1922. At the Bauhaus, he developed his colour and form theory, particularly in Point and Line to Plane (1926), which explored the psychological effects of lines and shapes, aligning with Gestalt psychology. Geometric forms, especially the circle, angle, and curve, became central to his work. His major painting Yellow – red – blue (1925), two metres wide, features a vertical yellow rectangle, an inclined red cross, and a large dark blue circle, with intricate black lines and coloured patterns, emphasizing form and colour relationships. Kandinsky was part of Die Blaue Vier (The Blue Four) with Paul Klee, Lyonel Feininger, and Alexej von Jawlensky, promoted by Galka Scheyer. After the Bauhaus moved from Weimar to Dessau in 1925 and then to Berlin in 1932, Kandinsky left Germany for France in 1933. In Paris, he created biomorphic forms with supple outlines, used original colour compositions inspired by Slavic folk art, and occasionally mixed sand into paint for texture. His final major works, Composition IX (1936) and Composition X (1939), feature powerful diagonals, contrasting colours, and enigmatic forms, with the latter showing star-like fragments and pastel hieroglyphs. He believed his forms were designed to resonate with the viewer’s soul. He wrote that "music is the ultimate teacher," and composed ten Compositions, of which the first three survive only in black-and-white photographs by Gabriele Münter. Composition I (1910) was destroyed by a British air raid on 14 October 1944 in Braunschweig. His first three Compositions were confiscated during a Nazi raid on the Bauhaus in the 1930s and destroyed during World War II. Some of his works, such as the now-lost Zweierlei Rot (191), are also missing. Kandinsky became a French citizen in 1939 and died in Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1944.

Kandinsky's artworks often feature large maroon masses positioned in the upper-left corner, with certain elements subtly veiled and only becoming apparent to viewers who engage deeply with his work. He designed his forms to resonate with the observer's soul, believing that art created from an internal necessity serves as a spiritual expression. Writing that "music is the ultimate teacher," Kandinsky created the first seven of his ten Compositions, with the first three surviving only in black-and-white photographs taken by Gabriele Münter. Composition I (1910) was destroyed during a British air raid on Braunschweig on the night of 14 October 1944. A Nazi raid on the Bauhaus in the 1930s led to the confiscation of Kandinsky's first three Compositions, all of which were later destroyed during World War II. Some of his works, like the now-lost Zweierlei Rot (1916), were displayed in the state-sponsored Degenerate Art exhibition, and works confiscated during this campaign were sold, exchanged, or destroyed; over 16,000 pieces, including Kandinsky's, are accessible via the Victoria and Albert Museum website. Influenced by Christian eschatology and the idea of a coming New Age, Kandinsky's first seven Compositions frequently explore the apocalypse, drawing on biblical stories such as Noah's Ark, Jonah and the whale, Christ's resurrection, the four horsemen of the Apocalypse, Russian folktales, and myths of death and rebirth—using these as symbolic archetypes rather than literal narratives. In his book Concerning the Spiritual in Art, Kandinsky described the artist as standing at the apex of a pyramid that moves upward, where what is once strange or avant-garde becomes common knowledge over time. He was aware of scientific advances and modern artistic developments. Composition IV and later works focus on evoking spiritual resonance, such as in Composition VI, which translates epic myths into contemporary terms of urgency and confusion. Kandinsky believed in synesthesia, expressing that yellow corresponds to middle C on a brassy trumpet, black to closure and the end of things, and color combinations to musical chords; he began playing piano and cello in 1871. He theorized that the circle is the most peaceful shape, representing the human soul, as detailed in Point and Line to Plane. His stage design for Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition, premiered in Dessau in 1928, illustrates his synesthetic view of forms, colors, and music, and was later animated in 2015 using modern video technology based on his notes and director Felix Klee's script. During work on Composition VI, Kandinsky became stuck and Münter advised him to repeat the word "uberflut" (deluge/flood) and focus on its sound, leading him to complete the painting in three days. Kandinsky's art combines music and spirituality, evolving from early expressionism through Art Nouveau, Fauvism, Blaue Reiter, Surrealism, and Bauhaus to abstraction, emphasizing emotional harmony and spiritual abstraction through color and form. His style is categorized into Impressions (representational), Improvisations (emotional), and Compositions (ultimate works). As he moved away from Impressionism, his paintings became more vibrant, pictographic, and expressive with sharp shapes and clear lines, eventually progressing to synesthetic, abstract compositions without depth or traditional references, yet maintaining a consistent spiritual pursuit. Emotional harmony is prominent in his later works, achieved through balanced proportions and bright hues, reinforcing the universality of form. He frequently used black to contrast brightly colored forms and employed biomorphic shapes to introduce surrealism. His theories on form and color stem from inner experience, not arbitrary associations, and involve years of observing his own and others' paintings to understand their emotional effects—an experience Michel Henry called "absolute subjectivity." Published in 1911, Über das Geistige in der Kunst defines three types of painting: Impressions based on external reality, Improvisations and Compositions emerging from the unconscious, with Compositions developed formally. After graduating in 1892, Kandinsky married his cousin Anja Chimiakina and became a lecturer in Jurisprudence at the University of Moscow. In 1902, he invited Gabriele Münter to join his summer classes in the Alps near Munich, and their relationship became personal. They became engaged in 1903 while he was still married to Anja, traveling across Europe, Russia, and North Africa until 1908. Münter bought a summerhouse in Murnau in 1909, which remained known as Russenhaus and was used to hide artworks from the Nazis. Kandinsky founded the Neue Kunstler Vereinigung in 1909. He returned to Moscow in 1914 with the outbreak of World War I, and tensions with Münter worsened due to his lack of commitment to marriage, ending formally in 1916 in Stockholm. In 1916, he met Nina Nikolaevna Andreevskaya, whom he married on 11 February 1917 when she was 17 or 18 and he was 50; they had a son, Wsevolod (Lodya), born at the end of 1917, who died in June 1920. After the Russian Revolution, he returned to Germany in 1920, teaching at the Bauhaus from 1922 until its closure by the Nazis in 1933. He moved to France with his wife, becoming a French citizen in 1939 and producing some of his most significant works there. He died in Neuilly-sur-Seine on 13 December 1944. In 2012, Christie's sold Kandinsky's Studie für Improvisation 8 (1909) for $23 million, previously on loan to the Kunstmuseum Winterthur since 1960 and sold by the Volkart Foundation; his previous record was set in 1990 with Sotheby's Fugue (1914) at $20.9 million. On 16 November 2016, Christie's auctioned Rigide et courbé (1935) for $23.3 million, a new record, originally purchased by Solomon R. Guggenheim in 1936 and not exhibited after 1949, later sold in 1964 by the Guggenheim Museum. In July 2001, Jen Lissitzky filed a restitution claim against the Beyeler Foundation for Improvisation No. 10, resulting in a 2002 settlement. In 2013, the Lewenstein family filed a claim for Painting with Houses held by the Stedelijk Museum; in 2020, a Dutch cultural committee found fault with the Restitution Committee, leading to resignations, and a court in Amsterdam ruled the museum could retain the painting despite Nazi theft, though in August 2021, the Amsterdam City Council decided to return it to the Lewenstein family. In 2017, Robert Colin Lewenstein, Francesca Manuela Davis, and Elsa Hannchen Guidotti filed a lawsuit against Bayerische Landesbank (BLB) for the restitution of Das Bunte Leben.
